resources.string: A qualitative view of normal adult teeth and chewing. The drawings show selected teeth and simplified jaw motion. Size and pacing are schematic.
In this view of the upper teeth from below, incisors line the front. A pointed canine sits on either side, followed by premolars and then broad molars. The highlight follows this order.
The lower jaw rises toward the upper teeth. The thin incisor edges meet the food from above and below, cutting off a piece.
A pointed canine can grip tough or fibrous food. When the food is pulled against the tooth, the fibers can stretch and part. This is one way a bite can separate.
Premolars and molars have broader chewing surfaces. The lower jaw rises and shifts slightly sideways. The back teeth press and slide against food between them, breaking it into smaller pieces.
Tongue and saliva help form a bolus

As the jaw opens, the tongue can guide food back onto the chewing surfaces. Saliva moistens the pieces so they can gather into a soft mass called a bolus. Teeth break food down mechanically; they do not digest it chemically.
